Introduction

From 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is said: "The Messenger of Allah drew a line with his hand and said: 'This is the way of Allah.' Then he drew lines to his right and lines to his left, and said: 'These are paths, and on each path there is a devil inviting to it.' Then he recited: '(And this is My straight path, so follow it, and do not follow other paths, lest you be separated from His path)' (1) (2)."

From this prophetic indication arose in me a desire to uncover one of these devils and his means of enticing people away from the straight path of Allah. This desire was strengthened by a firm belief born out of a long study in the science of theology and its results, that we must now conduct a critical review of the methodology of this science that we have adopted and relied upon in matters of belief, although it is not the correct scientific method, neither in proving those matters, nor in defending them, nor in calling to them, which are the purposes cited by those who defend this science, which has been inflated with issues that many of its masters and followers have long considered to be among the Islamic beliefs without which the Muslim's belief cannot be complete or valid, although they do not amount to anything more than ideas that have no connection to Islamic beliefs, or secondary issues that have turned, due to argumentation or prejudice or deception, into beliefs for which one is cursed and fought over, and for many centuries we have continued to chew over and ruminate on these ideas as if our nation has made argumentation an end in itself, until we have outpaced life while we remain as if time has frozen us in discussing issues from a corrupt heritage that we inherited or were inherited from previous nations. Since the first century, we have continued to circle around the issue of the attributes of Allah and their relation to Him and His creation, despite the fact that the Qur'an (1) Al-An'am 153 (2) Narrated by Ahmad, Al-Daraqutni, and Ibn Majah, and Al-Bazzar in his book Al-Sunna with a correct chain of narration.

It is said by Al-Maqrizi, 848 AH, explaining to us the full name of Ibn Saba: "And there arose in his time, that is, the time of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, 'Abd Allah ibn Wahb ibn Saba, known as Ibn al-Surda, the Sabian, and he introduced the claim that the Messenger of Allah explicitly appointed 'Ali as the Imam after him. And he introduced the claim that 'Ali returned and the earth is alive and that there is a divine part in him. And from Ibn Saba branched out the various groups of the Rafidha (28)."

These are sufficient texts to achieve our purpose in identifying Ibn Saba, and the historians and writers have not deviated, almost, from the content we have mentioned. However, none of them have given us the date of his birth or death, and their excuse for this is the method of Ibn Saba in secrecy, concealment, and the mystery that surrounded himself. What concerns us from this biography that we have presented, through the texts we have selected from the historians' words, is to identify his ideas, which are considered a part of his method of seduction and his method of seducing people with them until they became beliefs, and he became the source and nucleus around which sects formed in Islamic history, which form the general structure and the main basis for the method of the Sabians after him until now. As we have seen from his biography, he was the first innovator in Islam. But before we move on to his ideas, we would like to conclude our research into his biography by discussing two issues, the first of which relates to his existence as a historical reality, and the second relates to the difference between the moderate and the extremists among the Shia, which I mention here to clarify the intention and to prevent misunderstanding.

Gustave Le Bon says: "Some words and phrases have a power that neither reason weakens nor evidence affects. These are words and phrases spoken by a speaker prostrated before the masses, so that hardly have they left his mouth before the dignity rises on the faces of the listeners, and the faces turn to them in respect. And the idea of the veil and return, which Ibn Saba' proposed, is of that kind of words and thoughts! For the devoted follower always exaggerates in raising the one he loves or what he loves to extraordinary levels, as a psychological justification for himself and others for this exaggeration. This is an idea that the Sabians proposed as an explanation for gaps that appeared in the application of the theory of Imamate. 63:
The Bida'

It is another idea whose roots we are not concerned with tracing outside Islamic thought, which is the approach we have adopted in our research plan. Rather, we are concerned with its use and effects within this thought and its purpose. The practical application of Sabian ideas led to the advocacy of this concept. Thus, the bida' is considered a supplementary and supportive idea for the claim of taqiya, used for justification and deception. The first to present it in Islamic thought was Al-Mukhtar ibn Abi 'Amir al-Tha'labi, who began as an external figure, then switched to supporting Zubayr, then abandoned him to become a Khariji, claiming the imamate of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiya, and finally became a Sabian who claimed the transfer of imamate to himself, then claimed divinity. He said: "It is permissible for God Most High to change, and it occurs in three ways:

Change in knowledge. That is, God knows something, then something contrary to what He knew appears to Him.

Change in will: That is, He intends something, then something correct contrary to what He intended and ruled appears to Him.

Change in command: That is, He commands something, then something appears to Him, and He commands something contrary to it afterward.

All of this is confusion and lying about God to deny lying about himself. The reason he was led to claim it is that he claimed for his followers knowledge of what would happen, either through revelation from God to him or through a message from the Imam. So whenever he predicted something for them and it happened as he predicted, he would take it as proof of the truth of his claim. But if it happened contrary to his prediction, he would say: "Your Lord changed," mixing this with the permissibility of abrogation in rulings, saying: "If abrogation is permissible in rulings, then change is permissible in news."

69:
The Hermeneutic Method

We have seen previously that the first to establish a hermeneutic method in service of an opinion was Abdullah ibn Saba, who used it in his argumentation to plant the first idea in Islamic thought, the idea of occultation, by saying, as God Almighty says: "Indeed, He who has imposed the Qur'an upon you will surely bring you back to the Hereafter" (1). With this method of interpretation, Ibn Saba caused a revolution in the religious thinking of Muslims and affected all Muslims, near and far. Abdullah ibn Saba was the first to realize that all these ideas he planted in Islamic thought would remain limited in their impact unless they were based on a justification from the Qur'an. However, considering that he was a religious man and a learned rabbi from the rabbis of the Jews, knowledgeable about the philosophy of religious history, he must have known the extent of the obstacles standing between him and achieving his goal through these ideas, which appeared to him in two forms:

First: The Holy Qur'an, which God has promised to preserve: "Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will preserve it" (2), and God does not break His promise.

Second: The scientific method adhered to by the scholars of the righteous predecessors in matters of creed and occultations. This method is based on acceptance of revelation and refraining from debate about it, and it is the foundation of the religious and political unity of Muslims.

Thus, he found himself facing an inerrant Book, guaranteed by God's promise against alteration, substitution, addition, or omission, and facing a sound scientific method that protects Muslims from discord, deviation, and error. He found himself before God and a method of submission to Him, facing an impossibility, which is (1) Al-Qasas 85 (3) Al-Hijr 9.

77:
Falsifying Letters

The Sabaeans were the first to plant this vice in Islamic history, from which arose the audacity to fabricate in hadiths and news. In order to understand the effect of this method, we must observe the time and environment in which it was used. At that time, the measure of speed was the swift horse, and the means of communication to review and document news was slow. Moreover, the majority of the people were illiterate and did not know reading and writing. We must imagine the psychological effect that a written letter, the highest form of communication in that era, would have on an illiterate person like Sulaym al-Tawil, who did not know reading and writing. In light of this, we can estimate the danger of this method and its effect in sowing discord and sedition among Muslims. The Sabaeans used this method they invented with cunning and deceit in two fields: corrupting the relationship between the ruler and the ruled, and dividing the Islamic cities and sowing hatred and enmity between them. Let us take an example of their skill in using this method in creating the sedition of Uthman, which cost him his life and the unity of the nation with him, and we will leave to the historians to draw the picture of the events and the effect of the forged letters in shaping them.

Man does not fight for anything more than he fights for the creed he believes in. The stronger his faith in that creed, the more tenacious and fierce he becomes in defending it. When the Islamic nation used to adhere to a single creed, it was one nation in thought, values, ideals, and goals, united in behavior, weighing all matters by the standard of monotheism. They were brothers, rejoicing in the joy of their brother and grieving in his sorrow, loving what he loves and hating what he hates, angry at what he is angry at and pleased with what he is pleased with. They were a single nation in essence, like a building whose parts support each other, fighting in the way of God like a well-fitted structure. They used to encourage one another in all their affairs with truth and patience. Thus, the unity of creed is the only secret, apart from the analyses of analysts and the obscurations of philosophers, behind everything accomplished by our great and noble predecessors who mastered the crisis of history through their monotheism.

The unity of creed, or the unity of monotheism, is the foundation upon which the unity of the nation and its glory were built. The civilization of any nation is the fruit of its creed, and this is a fact attested to by history as well as by reality. It was from this foundation that the Sabians directed their tools of destruction, planting all sorts of ideas in Islamic thought, hoping that the nation's structure would collapse into ruins scattered by the wind. For when they succeeded in fracturing or weakening this creed, the nation fractured into sects and parties, and its resolve weakened, until it barely clung to the waning tail of history.

But Abdullah ibn Saba, in his time, knew that the ideas he had sown would bear fruit later, and he wanted to hasten the fate of this nation with his black hatred by killing its rulers and scholars, so that there would remain no pillar to which it could turn, no scholar to whom it could return. The other is this new path that the Prophet paved and his Companions raised its banners, which does not establish authority on strength, but rather on love and justice. It makes strength one of its tools and one of its means, and it knows no favoritism, no tyranny, and no coercion. It does not solve the problems of the world with worldly means, but rather with religious means, which are based on enjoining good and forbidding evil, on desiring good and shunning evil, on preferring others over oneself and renouncing favoritism. It relies, above all, on the purity of souls, the cleanness of consciences, and the purity of hearts. It takes the whole of this world not as a means to the Hereafter, which is not the case, but rather as a means to the Hereafter from one side, and as a means to a new world that becomes more refined, purer, and cleaner the more the days advance.

After the killing of Uthman, the Muslims found themselves at the head of these two paths. One of them said: "There is no harm in it for you, O Commander of the Faithful. As for the Battle of the Camel, which was the first general battle or civil war among the Muslims, it was all, cause and effect, the work of the Sabaeans. Its causes were in the fitna of 'Uthmān, which the Sabaeans created, and its results we will leave to the historians to recount their role in it. They say: that when the party of Talha and Zubayr and the Mother of the Believers 'A'ishah, who were seeking retaliation for 'Uthmān, had taken control of Basra, and the party of 'Ali, the Commander of the Believers, and those with him from the people of Kufa were before Basra, al-Qa'qa' worked for peace between the two sides to save the blood of the Muslims. When the mission of al-Qa'qa' ended with an agreement between the two sides to make peace and the people were all reassured, the conspirators feared the failure of their purposes, so they gathered under the leadership of 'Abd Allah ibn Saba' to consult on what they would do. One of them said: In my opinion, we should kill 'Ali and Talha so that this would be like that. The others rejected his opinion, because the aim was that the Muslims would destroy each other, and each one expressed an opinion. Then Ibn al-Su'dah said to them: If your strength is in the confusion of the people, then create confusion for them. And if the people meet tomorrow, then provoke the fighting and do not let them see clearly, so that whoever is with you will not find any way but to refrain, and thus preoccupy 'Ali, Talha, and Zubayr from what you dislike.

So when 'Ali wanted to enter Basra afterward, where the other army was, and the Sabaeans had plotted their matter without his knowledge or that of the rest of his army about what they were hiding, he sent to the people: If you are on what you parted from al-Qa'qa', then hold back and let us descend and we will look into the matter. So they descended and the people did not doubt the peace, and the envoys moved between the two sides, and the people spent the night waiting for safety.

The Muslims fought not for a right, but out of anger that filled the heart of each group because of the treachery of their enemy. All of them lost their minds and their sense, and the fitna (sedition) confused their affairs so that no one knew whether he was a killer or a killed, not caring why he killed or why he was killed. The matter did not leave room for anyone to think, and there was no opportunity to clarify the reality. This is what explains the intensity of the two sides in the battle, for each side believed the other to be treacherous. And nothing stirs up anger in the hearts of men more than treachery and betrayal, which are the most hated things to their souls. Thus, this disaster culminated in a day that the Muslims had never seen before in its horror and ugliness, a day in which the Muslims drew their swords against the Muslims, and in which the best of the Muslims were killed, the best of the companions of the Prophet, and the best of the scholars and reciters of the Muslims. The few historians say ten thousand were killed, and the many say fifteen thousand (13), and none of us looks at this number with the eyes of our time, as the Messenger said, "They are like the foam of a flood; every day, from the Muslims, people are killed in numbers many times greater than this." You will find among us someone who comments sarcastically, "This is a good solution to the problem of food, clothing, and housing," but let him look at it with the eyes of their time, when each one of them was equal to a nation in his knowledge, understanding, character, and valor. It has become clear to us from what preceded the method of the Sabians in deception and their goal in destruction. However, there remains a question that must inevitably come to mind after what we have presented, which is: How were the Sabians able to do all this? I have already mentioned that this call, by its nature, is a negative one, whose aim is to pursue the call to good in every time and place. And since Islam is the correct method for achieving this good, it was their traditional enemy, and their battle with it continued as long as it existed. And if every person knows or is able to know that the original founder of Islam is God, and that its preachers are the prophets and their successors among the scholars; because the call to good, by the nature of its objectives, is open, works in the light, and calls to it, then every person who cannot easily access this call, due to the nature of its hidden objectives and its reliance on secrecy in spreading these objectives, finds it difficult for many researchers to know its founder and preachers. Indeed, some of them even go so far as to doubt the existence of such a call with a founder, preachers, a method, and a goal, and consider all of that to be a kind of fantasy. And they have some excuse for that, first because of the irrationality of its objectives. It is difficult for a sane person to imagine the existence of those who intend evil for evil, for evil in itself is a negative, empty thing that does not suit achieving any positive goal. And second, because of the secrecy and strict confidentiality in which this call operates, which is considered an important part of its system. As for those who are aware among the scholars, they know from the Qur'an much about its founder, its preachers, its method, and its goal. And that it is exactly the opposite of Islam in method and goal. If the method of Islam in all ages elevates the human being to good, then the method of this call brings him down to evil. And if the goal of Islam is truth and good and the realization of human happiness, then the goal of this call is the opposite.

And as if I see with my own eyes the Sabians' attempt to seize control of this entire awakening, directing it to a goal opposite to that of the youth and the nation, using the same wicked method of deception and misguidance, but with a new approach based on:

First: Gaining the youth's trust by following their enthusiasm and sincerity in heading toward the Book and the Sunna, and showing great respect for religious texts, sanctifying them, and exaggerating in doing so, while at the same time they lead the youth to a corrupt method in dealing with these texts and deriving rulings from them. This is done by diverting them from the comprehensive or integrative method of looking at these texts to a partial method that looks at the texts in a one-sided way, invalidating the benefit from them or leading to erroneous rulings that the youth consider part of Islam, while they are not part of it at all. The features of this method become clear in the phenomena we see now in dealing with religious texts and the ways of using them, and we can take from them an indicator of the extent of the Sabians' success in using this method, such as:

  1. Dissecting the connections and objective unity of the texts in relation to a single subject or issue, by focusing attention and interest on one aspect of the subject or issue and neglecting the other aspects. For example, highlighting texts that speak about rights, while ignoring those that speak about duties.
112:
And neglecting the texts that speak about obligations, or focusing on intimidating texts without encouraging ones, or on vices without virtues, or on punishment without reward, or on fear without hope, or the opposite, and so on.
2 - Highlighting texts that speak about certain secondary issues, recommended acts, disliked acts, or special or exceptional rulings, and exaggerating the attention given to them in order to shift attention from beliefs to secondary issues, from obligations to recommended acts, from prohibited acts to disliked acts, from the general rule to the exception, or elevating secondary issues to the level of beliefs, recommended acts to the level of obligations, disliked acts to the level of prohibited acts, and the exception to the level of the general rule.
3 - The chaotic use of texts and deriving rulings from them, by pushing youth to rely on the literal meanings of texts in argumentation or deriving rulings from them, while neglecting to mention the conditions of this argumentation or derivation, or to point them out.

Secondly: Fragmenting the youth movement into separate groups, each group to which we send a suitable person who has the ability to gain their admiration and trust, entering into it through their religious emotions and their hopes for reform and improvement, by presenting an idea or issue that becomes the axis of their thinking and behavior. Justifying for them the acceptance of this idea with religious texts that he interprets to support his idea, until it becomes for them a belief and a religion by which they worship God, and a criterion for acceptance and rejection, love and hatred, calling to it and sacrificing for it, until these groups turn into warring sects, each with its own beliefs and methods, different or conflicting, each sect calling to what it believes in as the Islam that everyone must embrace and act upon, accusing the other sects of apostasy, blasphemy, and cowardice, sects that agree only on one thing: declaring the society and the ruler as the greatest tyrant, whose destruction and whose bloodshed will resolve all problems.

From here, before this blessed awakening turns from a constructive and progressive energy into a destructive energy,
113:
Al-Milla wa al-Nihla

Or the trinity, the trinity is a trinity.

By death, by the destruction and the collapse, I call with great sincerity and a feeling of danger from a sedition that leaves nothing behind:

First: To the sincere rulers of our nation and the leaders among us, that you catch up with this youth, the sincere to his religion and his nation, not by force, for force begets force and defiance and stubbornness, and not by flattery or sycophancy, for that will only beget recklessness and arrogance and conceit, but by good ability, and there is nothing upon you but to increase your knowledge of Islam in belief, in law, and in ethics, for in that lies the strengthening of your rule and the support of your strength and the proper guidance of that rule and that strength to what is good for you and good for your nation, and you will learn then that the whole nation, its youth and its elders, does not turn away from your leadership, so be their leader and their example in reform and reformation, for God brings about by the rule what cannot be brought about by the Qur'an.

A warning to them.

Second: A call to the youth, that you know that you are the guardians of the present and the hope of the future, and that the glory of Islam and its strength and the revival of its civilization, the civilization of truth and goodness which your ancestors were a strange example and a unique model in the world of yesterday, depends on your hearts and your minds and your hands, and you will learn that the limits of your responsibility do not end with the reform of yourselves or your nation only, but with the reform of the whole world which has long awaited a Muslim leadership to take it from error to guidance and from misery to happiness, so fill your hearts with love for Islam and your minds with knowledge of it, not only to distinguish between what you want and what is wanted from you, but so that Islam returns through you to the world of today as a strange example and a unique model to be measured by and followed, so blessed are those who are strangers.

Third: A call to the scholars of belief and principles in every Islamic university in the world, that you catch up with the nation and the world, for the problem that you must treat now is the difference in the standards and criteria for knowing the truth from falsehood and error from correctness in matters of belief and principles, and you are the reference and the people of knowledge in explaining these standards and setting them, so as a precaution.
114:
To Prevent Sedition and Avert a Great Catastrophe

To prevent sedition and avert a great catastrophe, I call you to a general conference to discuss three specific issues:

First: Determining and distinguishing between doctrinal and foundational issues and secondary issues.

Second: Establishing a clear criterion for disbelief and belief.

Third: Establishing a correct methodology for teaching doctrine and other religious sciences.

If you reach an agreement on these issues, it will become a consensus and a criterion by which the nation—whether ruling or ruled—distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and a standard for the youth to discern between those whom they wish to guide and those whom they wish to mislead.

O God, I have conveyed the message. O God, bear witness.

(Exalted is your Lord, Lord of majesty, above what they describe, peace be upon the messengers, and praise be to God, Lord of the worlds.) (1)
